To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) human and cynomologus macaque serum provides a reproducibly protective effect in mice exposed to aerosolised Y. pestis, 2) the efficacy of passive transfer of serum is dependent upon the mouse strain, and 3) passive transfer of human or cynomolgus serum is a valid surrogate for human clinical trials.

(1) Hsd:NIH-Swiss mice are a better animal model for passive transfer studies than the commonly used BALB/c mouse, and (2) the pharmacokinetics of human and cyno IgG are similar in Hsd:NIhs mice and humans, and in BALB/c mice and cynos, respectively.
the efficacy of primate humoral passive transfer in a murine model of pneumonic plague is mouse strain-dependent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an animal model to assess efficacy of a new plague vaccine.
the development of a novel vaccine against plague and the use of nonhuman primate passive transfer models to support its development and licensure.
the development of an acellular plague vaccine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

humoral passive transfer of serum from immunised cyno macaques to Hsd:NIH Swiss mice is an effective model for assessing the efficacy of plague vaccines in humans and is superior to BALB/c mice for these studies.
the Hsd:NIH Swiss mice are the best animal model for humoral transfer studies.
the use of human or nonhuman primate IgG as passive immunisation in a murine pneumonic plague model is an acceptable surrogate for human efficacy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of human and non-human primate serum in the murine model of pneumonic plague provides a reproducible and robust model for assessing the pharmacokinetics of human and non-primate IgG and for evaluating the efficacy of human and nonprimate passive transfer of immunity in the murine pneumonic plague model.
the Hsd:NIH Swiss mouse is a more appropriate model for passive transfer studies than the BALB/c mouse.

human and cynomologus macaque serum provides an effective means for passive transfer in the murine model of pneumonic plague, but the mouse strain used is important for accurate interpretation of the results.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of nonhuman primates in passive immunization studies is a valid approach to assess the potential of new biodefense countermeasures.
the use of human and non-human primate sera in animal models of plague is a valid and useful tool for vaccine development.
passive transfer of serum containing anti-rF1/rV IgG can be used as an assay of immunogenicity in human clinical trials of the rF1/rV vaccine.
